fields.title: Loading data
fields.description: Bricks that show other documents, such as the latest posts or a product grid.

data.source:
Some bricks show more than their own data: the newest posts, the products in a category. Give such a brick a `load` function. It receives the brick's data and a typed reader, and what it returns reaches the component as `props.loaded`. ```tsx export const latestPosts = defineBrick({ name: 'latest-posts', label: 'Latest posts', schema: { heading: fields.text({ label: 'Heading', default: 'Latest posts' }), limit: fields.number({ label: 'How many', min: 1, max: 12, default: 3 }), }, load: (data, content) => content.list(posts, { limit: data.limit }), component: (props) => (

{props.data.heading}

    {(post) =>
  • {post.fields.title}
    • }
), }); ``` Write `load` before `component`, so `props.loaded` gets its type. ## Where it runs - **On the server**, when the page renders, so the content is in the HTML. Pages that ship no JavaScript work too. - **In the admin preview**, in the browser. It reads saved content, and loads again after each save. It reads from the `ContentContext` your app provides. ## What makes it load again Read the `data` fields your loader depends on **before its first `await`**. Changing those fields loads again, and changing others doesn't. While a new load is in flight, the previous result stays on screen. A source can also offer `track()`: `PageView` calls it before each load, where reads are tracked, so reading a signal there makes every loader run again when it changes. The admin preview does this after saves, and this site does it to swap in your edits.

data.title: Return plain JSON
data.body: What `load` returns may be sent from the server to the browser with the page, so keep it plain data: no functions, class instances or promises inside.
